<margin>A</margin> we must do so. From where, then, do you wish us to begin our investigation? Since we have entered upon a certain model, so that we may see whether the names themselves will guide us in our inquiry, or whether everything is merely accidental and haphazard, or if they possess a certain correctness. Now, names given to heroes and men might perhaps deceive us. For many are given to them after the surnames of their ancestors, which have no relation to them, as we were saying at the beginning; and men often bestow names as though expressing a wish, such as <term>Eutychides</term> <gloss>son of good fortune</gloss>, <term>Sosias</term> <gloss>savior</gloss>, <term>Theophilus</term> <gloss>beloved of God</gloss>, and many others. Such names, then, it seems to me we ought to dismiss.
<margin>B</margin> It is most likely that we shall find names rightly established in those things that are eternal and naturally existing. For it is especially fitting that earnest care was taken concerning the imposition of names there. Perhaps some of them were even established by a power more divine than that of mortal humans. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak well, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not just, then, to begin from the gods, examining how this very name, the gods, was rightly called? **HERMOGENES:** It is reasonable. **SOCRATES:** Here is what I suspect. It appears to me that the earliest inhabitants of Greece considered those to be the only gods whom many of the barbarians still revere today: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Seeing that all these were always running in motion and running swiftly <note>original: "θέοντα"</note>, from this nature of running <note>original: "θεῖν"</note> they called them
<margin>C</margin> <margin>gods</margin> gods <note>original: "θεούς"</note>. Later, learning of the rest, they addressed all of them by this name. Does what I say seem like the truth, or not at all? **HERMOGENES:** It seems entirely like the truth. **SOCRATES:** What, then, should we investigate after this? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly both daimones, heroes, and men. **SOCRATES:** Daimones? And indeed, Hermogenes, what might the name daimones ever mean? Consider whether you think I am saying anything sound. **HERMOGENES:** Only speak. **SOCRATES:** Do you know, then, whom Hesiod says the daimones are? **HERMOGENES:** I do not call it to mind. **SOCRATES:** Nor that he says the golden race of men came first into being? **HERMOGENES:** That I do know. **SOCRATES:** He says of it, then: "Yet when fate covered this generation, they are called holy daimones dwelling upon the earth, noble, deliverers from evil, guardians
<margin>D</margin> of mortal men." **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** I believe he calls it the golden race not because it was made of gold, but because it was good and noble. My evidence is that he says we are an iron race. **HERMOGENES:** You speak truly. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think, then, that if someone living today were good, Hesiod would say that he belongs to that golden race? **HERMOGENES:** It is likely. **SOCRATES:** And are the good anything other than wise? **HERMOGENES:** Wise. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it seems to me, he calls them daimones above all because they were wise and knowledgeable <term>daēmones</term> <gloss>knowing ones</gloss>; he named them daimones, and in our ancient language the name itself coincides. Both he and many other poets speak well, all who
<margin>E</margin> say that whenever a good man dies, he obtains a great destiny and honor, and becomes a daimon, according to the surname of wisdom. In this way I myself also hold that every knowledgeable man who is good is daemonic <gloss>divinely inspired</gloss>, both living and dead, and is rightly called a daimon. **HERMOGENES:** I believe, Socrates, that I am entirely in agreement with you on this point. But what might a hero be? **SOCRATES:** That is not very difficult to grasp. For their name has been slightly altered, showing their birth from love <term>erōs</term> <gloss>love</gloss>. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that heroes are demigods? **HERMOGENES:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** All of them were surely born from a god falling in love with a mortal woman, or a mortal man with a goddess. If you examine this according to the ancient Attic dialect, you will understand better. For it will show you that from the name of love <term>erōs</term> <gloss>love</gloss>, whence the heroes were born, it is slightly altered for the sake of the name.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>from love</margin> And either it calls them heroes for this reason, or because they were wise, and rhetoricians, and skilled, and dialecticians, being capable of questioning <note>original: "ἐρωτᾶν"</note>. For to speak <note>original: "εἴρειν"</note> means to utter words. Just as we were saying just now, when called heroes in the Attic tongue, they turn out to be rhetoricians, questioners, and lovers, so that the heroic race becomes a family of rhetoricians and sophists. But this is not difficult to understand. Rather, regarding that of men, can you tell why men are called <term>anthrōpoi</term> <gloss>human beings</gloss>? **HERMOGENES:** How could I, good sir? Even if I were somehow able to discover it, I would not exert myself, because I believe you will be able to discover it better than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to place your trust in the inspiration of Euthyphro. **HERMOGENES:** Evidently. **SOCRATES:** And you trust rightly. For even now I seem to have thought of it cleverly, and there is a danger, unless I take care, that I shall become wiser today than is proper. Consider what I say. First,
<margin>G</margin> one must understand this about names: that we often insert letters and remove others, naming them as we wish, and we change the pitch accents. For instance, <term>Dii philos</term> <gloss>dear to Zeus</gloss>; so that this might become a single name for us instead of a phrase, we removed one iota from it, and instead of an acute accent on the middle syllable, we pronounced it with a grave accent. With others, on the contrary, we insert letters, and pronounce acute syllables more gravely. **HERMOGENES:** You speak truly. **SOCRATES:** In my view, this is the very thing that has happened to the name of men. For from a phrase it has become a name, with one letter, alpha, being removed,

# Third Instruction ( 122 )

### Root: Afterwards, one should perform the Bellows <term>Bhastrika</term> and quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term>. || 15 ||
### One should perform the contraction of the sun and then move the <term>Kundalini</term>. Even if one has entered the mouth of death, why should there be any fear of death? || 16 ||
### By moving the śakti fearlessly for the duration of two <term>muhurtas</term> <gloss>approximately 96 minutes</gloss>, it is drawn slightly upward, having arisen in the <term>Sushumna</term> <gloss>the central channel</gloss>. || 17 ||
### By that movement, the <term>Kundalini</term> certainly leaves the mouth of the <term>Sushumna</term>. Therefore, this life-breath <term>prana</term> enters the <term>Sushumna</term> on its own. || 18 ||

->|| Commentary ||<-

The word "afterwards" means having performed the previous actions. After the practice of moving the śakti <term>Shakti-chalana</term>, one should perform the <term>breath-retention</term> <gloss>kumbhaka</gloss> known as the Bellows <term>Bhastrika</term>. In this way, one should quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. Although the Thunderbolt Pose <term>Vajrasana</term> was already prescribed for the process of moving the śakti, it is mentioned again here to establish a rule: the Thunderbolt Pose must be maintained specifically for the Bellows breath following the energy movement. || 15 ||

Regarding the sun: One should perform the contraction of the sun, which is located in the region of the navel. This contraction of the sun occurs by the contraction of the navel itself. Then, from that contraction of the sun, one should move the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. For a man who performs this, even if he has reached the mouth of death, where is the fear of death or the fear of time? The meaning is that there is no fear at all. || 16 ||

Regarding two <term>muhurtas</term>: For a period of two <term>muhurtas</term>, which consists of two pairs or four <term>ghatikas</term> <gloss>a ghatika is 24 minutes</gloss>, the energy is moved fearlessly and without doubt. Through this, the energy arises in the <term>Sushumna</term> and is drawn slightly upward. || 17 ||

Regarding "by that": By that upward drawing, the <term>Kundalini</term> leaves the mouth—the entrance—of the well-known <term>Sushumna</term>...

->|| Vernacular Language ||<-

After performing the gesture for moving the śakti, one should perform the breath-retention named Bellows. By this method, one should quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. || 15 ||

Regarding the sun: One should contract the sun situated in the navel region. By contracting the navel, the sun is contracted. Following the contraction of the sun, one should move the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. Then a man who has reached the mouth of death will have no fear of time. || 16 ||

Regarding two <term>muhurtas</term>: By moving the śakti fearlessly for four <term>ghadis</term> <gloss>units of 24 minutes</gloss>, this energy rises in the <term>Sushumna</term> and is pulled slightly upward. || 17 ||

Regarding "by that": By pulling it upward, the <term>Kundalini</term> certainly <note>original: "निश्चय" meaning "certainly" or "with certainty"</note> clears its own path of entry into the <term>Sushumna</term>...

<summary>This page describes the transition from moving the Kundalini energy to performing the Bhastrika breath-retention while seated in the Thunderbolt Pose. These practices aim to clear the entrance of the central channel so the life-breath can enter and rise, effectively conquering the fear of death.</summary>

# THE BOOK

<meta>catchword: Monarchy</meta>

But know this: the food that a person eats and the "food" of **medicine** <note>original: *Artzney*</note> are not the same thing. That is to say, they are not of one essence or of one kind. The reason for this is that all food eaten is **simple** <note>original: *einfach*; meaning unified or undifferentiated in its raw state</note>. And even though it is split into the **two Monarchies** <note>The distinct physiological realms of men and women</note>, this division concerns only the medicinal powers, and not the food or nourishment itself. 

Although for women, food is more useful in many ways when it comes from their own Monarchy than from the male Monarchy, this is because of the **infirmities** <note>original: *gebrestens*; referring to the specific physical vulnerabilities or sicknesses a body may harbor</note> that the body carries with it, and not due to the nourishment itself. 

There is a **smith** and a preparer in the **stomach** <note>original: *Magen*</note> who makes human **flesh** <note>original: *fleisch*</note> from the food. Now, he has two natures within him and acts like a kitchen. One nature is such that if he is in a man, he makes male flesh from it; if he is in a woman, he makes female flesh from it. The food is unified and is human food, but the **Archeus** <term>Archeus; the "inner alchemist" that Paracelsus believed resided in the organs to separate the useful from the waste and direct growth</term> is the one who prepares it for the person within their own **Monarchy**. 

Therefore, the **physician** <note>original: *Arzt*</note> does not need to burden himself with worry over how to administer nourishment; his concern instead must be the **medicine**—that it be directed into its proper Monarchy. ...to be distinguished and completely delimited. That aspect's distinction, meaning its difference, is what is meant. Mentioning distinction should also be understood as striving to make one realize the negation of non-distinction. It is not something to be understood through this manifold nature itself, because what is external does not exist at all, being merely an imputation.

Through this, it is clarified: for perception, an external object exists, from which the appearance of that object becomes vivid, whereas for inference, it does not. That non-vivid aspect of its object arises solely from the power of its own latent impression <term>bīja</term> <gloss>seed</gloss>. Therefore, direct perception and inference are distinct in their essential nature, as explained above.

Alternatively, the object of comprehension for direct perception produces its own aspect appearing vividly in reality through its own nature; whereas that of inference, through that very continuity, produces a non-vivid aspect of an object and is thus comprehended through the nature of another. Some maintain that direct perception is also comprehended through the nature of another.

In that way, because direct perception and inference have distinct objects, they are also distinct in their own essential nature due to the distinctions in their natures, by virtue of the vivid and non-vivid aspects of their objects.

When it is asked, "Why, for what reason?", it indicates the definite assertion: for what reason is inference alone divided into two kinds by the distinction between inference for oneself <term>svārthānumāna</term> <gloss>inference for one's own benefit</gloss> and inference for others <term>parārthānumāna</term> <gloss>inference for the benefit of others</gloss>, whereas direct perception is not?

This will be explained: words intended to make others realize an object that one has directly perceived oneself, why are they not accepted as a second kind, direct perception for others?

To this it is said: "Because..." and so forth. Because the object of inference is a universal <term>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</term> <gloss>general characteristic</gloss>, words produce exactly the same inference in the mental continuum of the other person as occurred within oneself; therefore, it is logical that inference has two kinds. The object of direct perception, however, is a particular <term>svalakṣaṇa</term> <gloss>specifically characterized individual</gloss>. Regarding this, words cannot produce in another continuum the exact direct perceptual consciousness that occurred within oneself...

<summary>This text discusses Buddhist epistemology (pramāṇa), contrasting direct perception and inference based on their distinct objects (particulars versus universals) and vividness. It also explains why inference is divided into types for oneself and for others, whereas direct perception cannot be communicated directly to another person through words.</summary>
